nameStory: The Eastern Eyed Click Beetle gets its name from two distinctive features that make it instantly recognizable. Those large, oval black spots on its back look just like enormous eyes staring up at you - though they're actually fake eyespots designed to startle predators! The 'click' part comes from its amazing ability to flip itself right-side up with an audible clicking sound when it's stuck on its back.
description: This is one of New England's most impressive beetles, looking like nature decided to create a insect with built-in googly eyes. The Eastern Eyed Click Beetle is a large, robust beetle with a mottled gray and black body that's covered in fine, velvety hairs. Adults can reach up to 2 inches long, making them one of the largest click beetles you'll encounter. Their most striking feature is the pair of large, black eyespots on their thorax that give them an almost comical, wide-eyed appearance.

idTips.label: Fake eyespots
idTips.description: Two large, prominent black oval spots on the back portion behind the head that look like giant eyes staring at you - these are unmistakable and unlike any other New England beetle

idTips.label: Clicking ability
idTips.description: When placed on its back, it can flip itself over with a loud 'click' sound by arching its back and snapping its body straight - try gently flipping one over to see this amazing trick

idTips.label: Velvety texture
idTips.description: The entire body feels soft and fuzzy to the touch, covered in short, dense hairs that give it an almost carpet-like texture unlike most smooth beetles

idTips.label: Mottled coloring
idTips.description: Body has a salt-and-pepper appearance with gray, black, and sometimes white speckled patterns that help it blend in with tree bark

idTips.label: Size and bulk
idTips.description: Noticeably large and chunky compared to most beetles, with a robust, elongated oval shape that fills up your palm when held

habitat: Look for these beetles in mature hardwood and mixed forests throughout New England, especially areas with plenty of decaying logs and stumps. They're often found under loose bark of dead or dying trees, particularly oaks, maples, and other deciduous species where their larvae feed on rotting wood. Adults are frequently attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting during warm evenings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their pupal stage in late spring and may be found under bark or in rotting logs as they prepare for mating season.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most commonly seen, often flying to lights at night or found crawling on tree trunks and decaying wood during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, though they become less common as temperatures drop and they seek winter shelter.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark, in hollow logs, or buried in leaf litter, remaining completely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: When threatened, this beetle doesn't just rely on its fake eyespots - it can actually 'play dead' so convincingly that it will remain completely motionless even when poked, then suddenly spring to life and flip away with its signature clicking sound, startling predators (and curious humans) enough to make a clean escape!
confusionNotes: The large eyespots make this beetle nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England - no other beetle has such prominent fake eyes. If you see large black spots that look like eyes on a beetle's back, you've found an Eastern Eyed Click Beetle!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their somewhat intimidating appearance with those big 'eyes,' these beetles are completely harmless to humans and don't bite or sting. The eyespots are purely for show - a clever evolutionary trick called Batesian mimicry that makes predators think they're looking at the face of a much larger, more dangerous creature.
compareHints: This is the only eyed click beetle species in New England, making identification straightforward. Other click beetles in the region are much smaller and lack the distinctive eyespots, typically being plain brown or black without the mottled pattern. The combination of large size, fuzzy texture, and prominent eyespots makes this species unmistakable among all New England beetles.
